items.headline: Honest Conversations About AI in Film Often Feel Impossible. IndieWire and Andreessen Horowitz, Cultural Leadership Fund Tackled the Challenge
items.body_text:
No matter what side you come down on, there’s no denying that AI is the currently the most important conversation topic in the realm of filmmaking. The technology appears destined to transform the art form in the near future and is the biggest growth area for investment in independent film at the moment. Depending on who you ask, it’s either a revolutionary tool that will unleash our hidden potential or an existential threat that could take away the very essence of artistry.

That polarized thinking can make it difficult to have nuanced conversations about what film’s AI future can realistically look like. But at the Cannes International Film Festival, IndieWire and Andreessen Horowitz, Cultural Leadership Fund created a forum to do just that. We partnered to host “Music, Film & the New Storytelling Stack — Co-Authoring What Comes Next,” an event held at The American Pavilion that featured panels and demonstrations from artists on the cutting edge of AI in film.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Related Stories After Row K Collapse, Maude Apatow’s Directorial Debut ‘Poetic License’ Finds a New Home Kent Jones and His Love of Actors Make ‘Late Fame’ One of the Best Films of 2026

The first conversation convened a panel of storytellers and business leaders whose thinking about AI transcends the “with us or against us” mentality that we so often see. Cultural Leadership Fund partner Judene Small moderated a conversation that included Masters vs. Machine CEO Roahn Hylton, Krea founder and Chief Technology Officer Diego Rodriguez, and IndieWire’s Chris O’Falt. All spoke about balancing human artistry with AI tools — and stressed the importance of clarity on such a broad topic.

“I get particularly annoyed at the word ‘AI,’ because it means different things for different people. And it’s impossible to have a conversation when people are not speaking the same language,” Rodriguez said. “For some people it means a chatbot, for other people it means TikTok or a recommendation engine, for someone else it means a technology that can automate my labor, whereas for other people it means a new type of tool to enable artists. I think that as long as that’s not clear, we cannot even start having a conversation.”

O’Falt added that many of our conversations about AI are happening so early in the technology’s development process that we find ourselves reacting to the low level, gimmicky products that are unlikely to make their way into actual filmmaking. The actual AI integrations that could happen a decade from now are likely to look more similar to the tools that Hollywood has been using for years.

“It would be easier if we just thought of some of the things being done in AI as natural extensions of what we’ve been doing with CGI for a while. But the problem is, the minute you say AI you’re thinking of a bad Brad Pitt fighting Tom Cruise and the slop,” he said. “Creating a space where this can be talked about is very difficult. Because you’re talking about a world that is fueled by money. And then there’s an audience that the minute they hear it, are angry and turned off. So the question becomes, how do you even create the platform to have that conversation the way we talk about anything else?”

Hylton added that these conversations are not simply technological or economic: they’re philosophical. He argued that AI art has such a visceral impact on people because it seems to threaten our very definitions of being human. He doesn’t see that as the only endpoint, but he stressed that AI advocates have to acknowledge those fears in their counterarguments.

“As humans, we want our art to cost us something,” he said. “We can relate to hard work. We can relate to putting time into something and getting a return. And that cost is threatened when you have a platform that you can prompt and then you see something… We’re having really high level existential questions about what it means to be human and how valuable are experiences are.”

The notion of collaboration between human artists and AI technology was on full display during a musical performance from Hylton and a live cellist, with Rodriguez generating live images using Krea along with the music in real time. The performance illustrated how AI can enhance traditional art forms, rather than simply replacing them.

The conversation soon turned to a more practical, pressing issue: copyright. Many artists worry about their work being used to train AI models without compensation, and technological advances in the field have been outpacing the legal developments. But the panelists noted that there are also plenty of positive examples of AI helping creators protect their own work.

“I am so annoyed at the fact that regulators and IP owners think of AI as an enemy as opposed to a tool,” Rodriguez said. “I’m like ‘did you know that you can use AI to detect your IP at scale and tell if it’s being infringed?’ So now AI can literally help you find IP infringement.”

Small added that the infancy of AI could lead new infrastructure that might share the fruits of the entertainment industry more equitably than in the past. She argued that rather than fighting over whether Silicon Valley or Hollywood sees more of the profits from AI projects, this is the time for conversations about letting creators get in on the ground floor.

“It feels like a false decision,” she said. “Silicon Valley is getting the big meat of the pie, but before Silicon Valley, who was making those decision? When you think about where capital is centered, there are always those individuals who are filtering down and giving us a false sense of real participation. And I think that’s why this conversation is happening, because there are builders and creators and toolmakers that are saying ‘Hey, this is a very early industry… it is ripe for all of us to participate in the infrastructure building.’ At the end of the day those decisions are being made on the artist side and on the tech side. And then it is influencing, thorugh capital, what is happening on the regulatory side.”

Finally, attendees had a chance to witness another demonstration that combined AI and human artistry when Dave Clark, the co-founder and Chief Creative Officer of Promise Studios, took the stage. Clark joined Smalls for a fireside chat about his journey with AI that led him to found a new entertainment studio for the AI age.

Before demonstrating AI-assisted work that Promise Studios did on a Coca-Cola ad, he explained his journey through traditional film school and his early years in Hollywood, where he was frequently told that his ideas were too large for his relative inexperience as a director. Clark explained that using AI tools to make his short film “Silent Valley” landed him a meeting with Ridley Scott, who echoed his belief that AI tools ultimately serve human storytelling processes.

“For him, it wasn’t about how it really looked. Because three years ago those tools were just, whatever. It was about the story,” Clark said of his meeting with Scott. “‘He goes, you found a way to take a tool that nobody knows what the hell it really does and get your story out there.’ There would be no way in hell I’d be able to do that and show that type of storytelling without the tool. But it was nothing without ten years of dedication of researching history and learning about the story that I wanted to tell that made the tool enable me to be the filmmaker I needed to be.”

The scope of the event, and the wide range of perspectives on display, confirmed how early we are in the AI process and how much we still have to learn. But the conversations also illustrated just how much nuance there is to the topic once we look past binary arguments about it. In her opening remarks, Smalls said that “the Cultural Leadership Fund is really dedicated to those who are shaping and building culture” and giving them a chance to share the financial gains they usher in. The day’s events made it clear that no matter what happens, the fund is well on its way to advancing that goal.

images.cap: Judene Small, Chris O'Falt, Roahn Hylton, Diego Rodriguez and David Clark on stage at the American Pavilion in Cannes

items.headline: Snapchat Banning Entirely AI-Generated Videos From Its Spotlight Platform
items.body_text:
As short-form digital video appears to be heading toward a wave of AI-generated slop, Snapchat is setting new ground rules for how that sort of content can exist on its platform moving forward.

The tech company on Friday said that it will ban wholly AI-generated videos in its Spotlight product, which surfaces trending and original content from creators and studios.

“As low-quality, repetitive, AI-generated content becomes increasingly common across the internet, we want Spotlight to remain a place where people can discover authentic creativity from real people, because we believe there’s enduring value in rewarding original perspectives, personal storytelling, and the moments that people choose to create and share themselves,” the company said in a statement.

AI is not banned altogether: Snapchat says that creators who have “enhanced or edited using Snapchat’s AI creative tools” will still be eligible for Spotlight, noting that “for some, AI plays an important part of the creative process, and we believe it can unlock incredible new forms of expression.”

Nonetheless, banning entirely AI-generated videos is meant to crack down on prompt-driven slop, which has become more prevalent on every platform as video models like Google’s Nano Banana and Seedance get better and better.

It also seems like something of a pushback against Facebook and Instagram, which have been more open to AI content.

In fact, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote in a post Thursday that the company’s Muse image and video models could lead to a “nearly infinite universe of personalized content.”

“This is going to make our services a lot more useful and engaging for people,” he added.

Snapchat seems to be betting that maybe humans will prefer something a little more human-led, even if AI isn’t cut out from the process entirely.

images.cap: The Snapchat app logo, illustrating Snap's new Spotlight rules on AI-generated video

items.headline: SeedDance 2.5 Just Got Upstaged by Nvidia
items.body_text:
It's been a wild week for AI news. There's a brand new tool that allows you to upload a single video clip and then move around in 3D space. Removing objects and re-lighting your video clips has never been easier and cheaper. And if you thought Seed Dance was impressive, let me show you this new model coming from NVIDIA. We have all of that along with 20 pieces of AI news you probably missed. Let's get to it. So, we're going to kick things off by talking about some news that we kind of hinted at last week. There's a brand new tool that allows you to upload a single video clip and then navigate in 3D space. The new tool is called InSpatio 4D Gaussian Splats, and you basically have the ability to take a single video clip and then upload it to create a 3D environment that you can actually move around. So, if you remember last week, we took a look at a tool that basically did the same thing, but you had to have an array of cameras to shoot all sorts of different angles.

This one's a little different. It actually uses AI to guess what is on the other side of the subject so that you can move around in a hybrid 3D world environment. It reconstructs the 3D geometry, the camera movement, and the objects' motion. And the cool part is you can play around with this today. So, for example, this scene is coming from a reference video of this woman pouring orange juice into a glass, but we can use our arrow keys here to move around in 3D space. So, it's almost like we were there on set and we're able to change the camera angle and change the overall direction. We also have this shot here of these kids reading a book, and we can move the camera around and tilt down and tilt up. And again, all of this is in real time. Obviously, the quality isn't quite production ready just yet, but the fact that you can do all of this from a single video clip is pretty wild. I think tools like this just reinforce that the future of creative video production is absolutely going to incorporate 4D Gaussian splats.

Everything from virtual production and visual effects to post-production is going to be transformed with this technology. I think there's a really good chance that over the next few years, you're not going to need of multiple camera angles. You're just going to need one really good performance with a primary A camera and then AI can infer the rest of the details if you want to go in and change your camera angle. Now, not to be outdone, the team at Adobe also released some research with their own version of a 4D world environment. The new project is called Project Wonder and it's a real-time AI tool that turns a single image or video into an interactive 3D environment that you can navigate. So, very similar to In paint. Now, Adobe doesn't have an interactive demo that we can play around with, but they do have a research paper that you can see a few different examples. So, for example, we have this shot here of this fantasy environment and you can see that Wonder does a really good job at generating the 3D assets in real-time.

It also can convert images into a 3D video world and so we have this anime scene here that we can navigate and get super close to our character. Again, it's not necessarily in what I would call photorealistic live-action real-time here, but it is pretty darn interesting and it will only get better from here. We can also simulate real-life environments. So, we have this woman drinking coffee here and then we can just navigate around and take a look at the view here and it's pretty crazy. Like you just have the ability to look around in real-time and explore the world as if you're there. And the other cool thing is you can do really complex camera movements that would be pretty hard to pull off on a normal production. So, for example, we can do this drone shot here of this environment that we have literally never visited, and you can see you can move the camera in all sorts of different directions, and it will generate the parts of the scene that you couldn't see from the starting camera angle.

And then finally, to illustrate what we were talking about earlier, we have this video footage of this guy who's basically doing a cooking segment, and we can just change the camera angle, and we can go in and out. You can really move around the scene in whichever direction you want. We also have this shot of this person doing yoga for I guess an influencer video, and again, you can move around the 3D scene. It's really, really cool. Or we have this shot of a band playing here, and again, we can move the camera around to get coverage of the band playing from different camera angles from a single reference video. It's pretty nuts. I think the fact that so many creative tools seem to be talking about 4D world models really implies that that is the future of where we're going over the next few years. The team at Midjourney has released their latest AI image model, Midjourney 8.2. In this brand new model, the team says that the images should be more creative, bold, sophisticated, edgy, and fresh, but we'll of course test that for ourselves.

They also said that the random situations where you get really low-quality images should be dramatically reduced, and the personalization will understand your taste much better, which is really helpful because a lot of times it can be a little too out there whenever you're trying to get something that is in your specific style. And they also said that the personalization feature will understand your personalized style much better. To use Midjourney 8.2, all you have to do is go to the Midjourney website, and we'll go ahead and paste in a quick little prompt here. Basically, I want to have a shot of a woman holding a glass orb with the words North Star into the surface of that orb. And we'll go to our settings here and make sure that we are in 8.2. And when you're ready, go ahead and click render. And after a few seconds, we have a few different images here. Image number one, which looks okay. The text is a little strange. We have image number two, which looks really cool.

I like that the actual text is out of focus. It feels like it is composited into the scene in a much more naturalistic way and it did a really good job. Much, much better improvement to the model all around. We also have this one, which I don't know if it did a very good job. It's kind of interesting, but not exactly what we're looking for. And then finally, we have this shot here, which again is okay, but not the best. Now, let's compare that against Midjourney 8.1, which gave us this image, which I do like, but it's not exactly what we're looking for. I would say that it feels like it was etched on the surface, but it's also living inside the orb. So, it's just a little odd here. And if we compare it against Midjourney 7, it's not really close. Midjourney 7 did a pretty bad job. The compositing on the text is not great, but also, look at that woman's fingers. Something horrible has happened here. Now, let's compare this against GPT-2, which is one of the more intelligent AI image models on the market.

In GPT-2, we got this image here, which in some parts looks good, but it really does come across more as stock photography and the outlines on the text is just overly sharp and it has this distortion that is really hard to explain. It's almost like a fractaling that you'll see on the details on the woman's face that just come across as fake. It's not quite realistic, not exactly what we're looking for. Technically, it's what we prompted for, but not as realistic as those cinematic details that you're so used to getting inside of Mid Journey. And we wanted to take it one step further, so we prompted for an image of a man in a denim jacket with a sign that says no entry. And this is what we got from Mid Journey 8.2. It looks so nice. The color grading looks very filmic. You can even see just grain texturing in the image. I think it did an amazing job here. And if we compare it against Mid Journey version 7, again, version 7 is okay, but it just comes across as a little staged and awkward.

It's not exactly realistic. In GPT-2, we got this image here, which again just comes across as very staged. It's not exactly cinematic. It doesn't have that depth that would help the image feel more realistic. It feels very much like stock photography. And we also wanted to compare that against Reeve, which is a very intelligent model that we've been really impressed by over the last few weeks. And in Reeve, we got this shot here, which again looks very good. In fact, I would say that the character himself probably comes across as more realistic than most of the other shots. There's definitely really fine details, especially in his skin textures and the hair that I really, really like. The problem is the overall staging and color grading again feels very stock photography-esque, even though we prompted for something cinematic. We also prompted for a cinematic scene of a couple dancing close together, and then I had more supporting details about what I wanted to see from the specific shot.

And in Mid Journey 8.2, we got this shot here, which looks really nice. I think it did a very good job. My only feedback is it seems like the guy is wearing a suit on his right arm, and then the left arm does not have a suit. So, unless that's a really experimental and interesting clothing choice, I think it's kind of missing the mark here. In Midjourney 7, this was the best shot, which again looks very good, but the skin is slightly plasticky. So, it's not exactly 100% realistic. In GPT-2, we got this image, which looks like a still from an actual film. It did an amazing job. And then finally, inside of Reeve, we got this image here, which again did a really decent job. Although, I do think that the skin texturing is a little soft. It almost looks like somebody went into Photoshop and just smoothed out the skin a little too much. Now, let's take a look at a couple of non-cinematic examples to see if Midjourney 8.2 still stacks up. So, we prompted for an image of a disposable camera photo of a group of friends at a house party, again with more supporting information that I'm not going to read off in this video.

And in Midjourney 8.2, we got this image, which at a quick glance looks incredible. [music] There's all of the texturing and color grading and compositing that you would want to see from an image like this. I think the only thing that feels off is the guy's hand in the background. I'm just not entirely sure what's going on there. It's like it just kind of started morphing into just kind of some weirdness there. So, I think we would need to test this with a few different images before we could use it in an actual project. In Midjourney 7, we got this image here, and I'm not entirely sure what's going on with those solo cups in the background. They're kind of stacking weird. So, there's definitely some stuff that's off as well. Now, in GPT-2, we got this image, which does look kind of realistic at a quick glance, but again, it has that fractaling problem. Do you see that grain texture? It's really present in a lot of GPT-2 image generations.

I'm not entirely sure why. And then finally, this is the same result that we got from Reeve, which I don't know if this comes across as a disposable camera. It almost looks like it was shot on like a DSLR. Now, the biggest problem is grain texturing. Again, in the background, you see we have the blank wall, and the grain is very inconsistent, which isn't necessarily a huge problem. You might see something like that in the scanning processes with a disposable camera. But, if we zoom in on the people's faces, it's actually super clean. It's almost like it's mixing in different styles into the overall image. And so, it's not exactly giving us the image that we're looking for. And the final test that I wanted to check out is the creation of a band poster. So, we prompted for a very long prompt, essentially of all the information that we would want to see from a poster that could be hypothetically printed out to promote an upcoming show. And inside of Midjourney 8.

2, we got this generation here, which looks really cool. Stylistically, I think it's awesome. Obviously, there's a lot of text in here, and it pulled it off pretty well. funny thing is, it did add in an additional in into the generation. So, you'd probably have to prompt it a few times to fix any sort of issues that you see inside of the generation. But, altogether, I really like it. It definitely has this organic feeling to it that you're not getting in a lot of other AI image tools. Now, again, let's compare that against Midjourney 7, which gave us this. And if you look at various text throughout the image, it's just a bunch of nonsense. So, not really what we're looking for. In GPT-2, we got this image here, which again looks really nice. But, I've noticed that a lot of times whenever you generate an image, like a graphic design concept, inside of GPT-2, but I have noticed that when you're generating body text on a graphic design poster inside of GPT-2, it almost always will add just a little bit of a serif in this specific font.

I don't really know what I would call this font, but it's almost like the most basic version of a sans-serif font that has just little edges of serif attached to it. And you see it all over the place. I've seen so many posters that have that exact same font, and it's so obvious every single time you see it that the image was generated in GPT-2. So, I guess next time you see an image and you're wondering if it was generated using AI, just look for those little little serifs at the end of the tall block text. finally, we got this image from Reeve, which Reeve is specifically designed for graphic design and text-based image generation projects. And I think it did the best out of all of these. Now, I do think you could weigh the pros and the cons stylistically between Midjourney and Reeve, but from a strict text adherence perspective, Reeve did a much much better job. Now, what is true of this image was also true of the photorealistic images that we got from Reeve.

If you notice, there's a lot of texturing in the background. So, there's something going on below the surface where Reeve is adding in a bit more noise, and it's creating a bit more texturing to the overall image, but the end result is an image that is very much in line with what you prompted. So, it's kind of a pro and con. And so, if you were to use this on an actual project, you may need to clean it up in a tool like Topaz to get exactly what you're looking for. So, all things considered, Midjourney 8.2 is a much faster and more accurate tool for image generation in a filmmaking and creative context. I don't think it's the very best tool every single time, and you're still going to have some consistency issues in Midjourney that you're not going to have inside of other omni-based image generation models like Nano Banana Pro or GPT-2. But I think if your goal is maximum cinematic realism or creative exploration, Midjourney is still the best tool on the market.

The team at LTX has released an open-source version of 2.3 that allows you to upload a video clip and remove people from the video. Essentially, you can get an automatic clean plate in just a few seconds. You can download this tool and run it locally on your computer, or you can use the online hugging face that I'm going to demo for you right now. So, I'm on the hugging face instance here, and first things first, we need some video footage. So, I have the shot from Artlist of these people having tea in this awesome awesome room. And let's say that for whatever reason, let's say we're working on a visual effects piece, and let's say that we want to remove the subjects very easily from this video clip. So, I'm going to drop the video clip into the LTX environment here, and you can see you can generate a video clip up to 10 seconds long. And you can output up to 960p. Again, that's not exactly HD, so it may be hard to use this in a professional visual effects workflow, but it's close.

And when you're ready, go ahead and hit generate clean plate. Now, we did generate in a lower resolution, so we could walk through a few different examples with you today, but whenever we generated in LTX, it gave us this video clip here, and yeah, the people are removed from the scene. Now, we did the exact same thing in SeedDance. So, we took the original video clip of the two people drinking tea, and then we just asked SeedDance to remove the subjects, and it gave us this, which actually did a better job. So, in this case, I would absolutely use SeedDance over LTX. For this shot, we have this random guy doing, I don't know what, in front of the camera here, and we wanted to remove him using LTX, and we got this, which, okay, yeah, did a pretty good job. He's gone. But, inside of SeedDance, we got this shot here, which looks really good. Look at the way the lens flare feels like it's connected to the sun. It all comes across as just much, much more realistic.

So, it did a really good job. We have the shot here of this guy doing yoga in the desert, and in LTX, it generated this clean plate, which has the camera motion in there as well. Not too shabby. And then we prompted for a clean plate from Seed Dance and got this. Do you get it? It's literally a clean plate. We prompted for a clean plate and it put a clean plate in the desert, which is hilarious. 10 out of 10 Seed Dance. No notes. >> [laughter] >> And then finally, we have this shot of this woman running. There's motion blur, camera shake, the background is like moving around. This would be so hard to do in a traditional visual effects environment. Now, we ran it through LTX, and LTX gave us this, which is okay. Like we have the reflections even with the the background down there. Not too bad. Obviously, I'm looking for more resolution, but we ran the same thing through Seed Dance 2.0, and that gave us this. And this is much, much better.

You would definitely need to onion skin this, where you take two video clips, put them on top of each other, and make the top one 50% opaque, just to double-check that all of the assets and the tracking is as accurate as possible. But again, Seed Dance did a much better job here. Now, that's not the only news from LTX. The team also came out with a re-lighting tool that allows you to upload a video clip and then change the time of day. So, let's take that last example of the woman running. You know, it's an overcast day. Let's make it sunny. So, we'll go ahead and drag and drop her into the source video section here. And what's kind of cool is you can change the overall angle of the light on your subject, which is kind of a cool little feature here. And you can go into much more detail about what you want the overall lighting style to be. They have this drop down here where you can select all sorts of different presets along with changing the angle.

But for our example, I'm going to go ahead and turn this up to 5 seconds, which is the maximum duration, and go ahead and hit relight video. And after a few minutes, LTX gave us this, which yes, it's technically relit, but also that character looks super wonky. Now, let's compare it against SeaDance where we prompted for a lighting change, and SeaDance gave us this, which yeah, that is the subject that was from the original video. I should note that a lot of the more realistic camera shake and motion blur is not as present in this generation. So, I wouldn't necessarily call every generation you're getting from SeaDance production-ready, but it is much better than LTX again. Let's take our shot of our yoga guy here, and let's move the sun to the background. And inside of LTX, we got this, and I don't know why it added in balloons, but it did. So, yeah, that's not what we're looking for, and that is definitely not the same environment. Like, it literally put him on the beach, which the original shot, he was not on the beach.

So, I'm not too sure what's going on there. Inside of SeaDance, we got this generation, which looks much much better. So, good job inside of SeaDance. Let's take a look at two final examples here. So, we have the shot of this woman, and you can see it's kind of sunset. And inside of LTX, we wanted to change it to midday, and we got this shot, which is pretty good, and actually, you may expect the opaqueness of that cloth to change based on the direction of the lighting in the background. So, maybe it actually did a decent job, but it is very, very low resolution. And if we compare that to the same shot inside of SeaDance, again, I think Seedance did a better job. I think with all of this being said, LTX is still an interesting tool because it's open-source. You have the ability to download it and run it locally on your machine. Even though it's not quite as good as the cutting-edge video models that you're probably going to see from updates from Kling and Seedance and other AI video tools, the fact that it's completely free if you put it on your machine makes it very interesting.

And also the fact that it can be integrated into ComfyUI pipelines makes it also very interesting in a larger production environment. In the creative AI world, typically when there's a brand new video model, like let's say Seedance 2.5, everybody freaks out and gets super excited. Well, today I have a model that I want to show you that is infinitely more important than Seedance, and it's absolutely going to change the way that we approach our projects forever. The tool is called Cosmos 3 Super from Nvidia, and it's basically an update to the Cosmos project that's already been going. This model is an AI world model that is open, meaning it can be downloaded and used on a machine locally, and it's 25 times faster than other models on the market. That's not the interesting part, though. The value proposition of this model is it gives you the ability to upload any type of data. So, that could be an image, a document, a video, an audio clip, or even physical movement from a robot or a human, synthesize that data, and output in any format.

This means you can put any data or database into this model, it will run it through the Cosmos 3 Super model, and output the data in any type of output. So, that could be an image, a video, an audio clip, or even instructions into a robot to do something. And the crazy thing is this model is not just a play toy. It actually ranks number one for open weight models for image to video and [music] text to image. There's a lot of reasons as to why this is truly mind-blowing, but one of them is it gives robots the ability to communicate with you a human through a creative and visual means as opposed to just text alone. If the robot is going to perform an action, it can create a video or an image or a document explaining what it's about to do. And on their website, they have a few different examples of this in action. Maybe it's the robot generating an image showcasing what design schematics it's going to begin working on. There's also shots of robot arms working in factories and this really terrifying image here of this robot holding a knife.

And the video model is really impressive as well and I don't know why more people aren't talking about it. So, we have this shot here of these humanoid robots on Mars and yeah, the physics look pretty nice and comparable against some of the other better video models on the market. We have the shot here of a little delivery robot in like a dystopian future here. And yeah, there he goes. And we have this shot here of this robot arm holding an apple and putting it down and yeah, it's pretty realistic. We have this shot of a car driving along a highway. We have this shot of a robot running and yeah, feels like there's weight behind the steps. It's doing a pretty decent job. There's a good reason why Nvidia is the most valuable company in the world and it's because they're working on stuff like this. If an AI system has the ability to generate synthetic data that is photorealistic, then it can begin to train itself on that data. Obviously, you need checkpoints in place and probably some level of human oversight to make sure that that data is as accurate as possible, but the fact of the matter is as more robotics are released into the world, having an efficient world model running beneath the surface is going to be key.

Up to this point, a lot of AI has kind of felt like a chatbot experience, but once we evolve past the chatbot and we can interface with our AI system, whether it's through simple voice commands or more realistically some sort of command that you don't even have to articulate, it's going to be a wild time. And the other thing that, again, we have to reiterate is these world models are the future of AI filmmaking and creativity. We're going to look back on the last 3 years and the next 2 years and remember the time when we had to use a specific tool for a specific task. In the very near future, there will be a single interface that you can use and get 99% of the outcomes that you're looking for. If you work with a lot of creative clients, especially in an advertising capacity, there's a good chance you kind of do the same thing again and again.

items.headline: Tech Reviews: Blender 5, Silhouette 2026 and DaVinci Resolve 21
items.body_text:
Blender 5.0

Blender 5.0 has been trying to earn something for years now. Not market share, not awards, but the trust — the specific, hard-won trust of the production pipeline, where color space mismatches cost money and integration failures cost time. That kind of credibility does not come from a single headline feature. It accumulates.

The most significant work in the latest release of the free, open-source software (best known for being used on Oscar-winning feature Flow) happens in the color pipeline. Improved HDR support, expanded color management options and continued development of the AgX view transform are not the kind of improvements that get a standing ovation at a product launch. But they matter enormously to anyone trying to hand off Blender renders to a Nuke compositor or round-trip plates through a DaVinci Resolve grade. For years, “close enough” was the answer to questions about Blender’s color behavior. Version 5.0 is trying to make that answer unnecessary.

Cycles gets faster. That sentence has appeared in Blender release notes for several versions now, but it remains true and worth saying. GPU optimization and physically based rendering refinements keep the renderer competitive with better volume rendering, more accurate subsurface scattering and expanded shading capabilities. Eevee continues its own quiet evolution, moving further from preview-mode stopgap toward a real-time renderer that artists might actually choose on its own merits.

Geometry Nodes is where Blender’s ambitions are most visible. The procedural system has been expanding version after version, pulling the software toward a way of working — nondestructive, modular, repeatable — that Houdini made famous and that more artists want access to. The difference is that Blender arrives at that philosophy without the price tag and without the assumption that the user has already committed years to learning a deeply particular way of thinking. The ceiling is lower, but the floor is much more accessible.

The surrounding infrastructure keeps pace: compositing improvements, better USD support, viewport performance gains and interoperability refinements that make moving between applications feel less like translation and more like handoff. Blender 5.0 is not trying to be everything. It is trying to be something that fits cleanly alongside the tools that already are.

For studios that have been watching Blender from a professional distance, wondering when “open source” stops being the asterisk next to every recommendation — this is a release worth reassessing. The gap is closing, and it is closing in the right places.

Website: blender.org

Boris FX’s Silhouette 2026

Roto work has a specific quality of misery when it goes wrong. Not dramatic misery — no explosions, no catastrophic failures. Just the slow accumulation of frames, edge problems, temporal flickering and the particular frustration of watching a shape that was working perfectly in the middle of a shot fall apart at both ends. Silhouette 2026 is a release that understands this misery specifically and addresses it without pretending the problem can be automated away.

The expanded AI tool set updates to FaceML, Depth Map ML, Mask ML, Matte Assist ML and Matte Refine ML — are built around a realistic premise: Artists still need to drive the process, but the repetitive parts of that process should not require the same attention as the creative ones. The improvements show up in edge quality, in motion-blur handling, in temporal consistency across frames. They show up in the shots that used to send roto artists into a second or third hour of cleanup work.

Tracking in Silhouette has always been functional. In 2026, it becomes genuinely useful on difficult shots. Point Track ML handles occlusions and reentries with more stability than previous tools allowed. Object Tracker can identify and generate tracked layers automatically, which means the setup work that used to precede roto sessions can now run concurrently with the artist’s first pass. The time saved is not dramatic per shot. But across a sequence, it adds up quickly.

The 3D workflow additions are where Silhouette 2026 moves most decisively into territory it did not previously occupy. Head Track ML generates a tracked 3D head mesh with expressions and pose data. The new Unwrap and Rewrap nodes connect that 3D information to 2D paint and roto work in ways that previously required moving between applications. For facial replacement, digital makeup and beauty work at high standards, this creates a more continuous pipeline inside a tool that artists already have open.

The 3D Scene improvements — powered by Boris FX SynthEyes technology — include a Refine Solve workflow that lets artists improve existing camera solves without throwing them out and starting over. This sounds like a small thing. Ask anyone who has had to re-solve a camera because a late element got added to the shot and it stops sounding small.

Paint artists get Healing Brush improvements and enhanced cloning tools that make everyday tasks faster. These are not headline features. They are the kind of refinements that only people who do paint work for a living will fully appreciate, which is exactly the right audience for Silhouette to be paying attention to.

Pipeline integration improvements — stronger Cryptomatte support, faster playback on AI-heavy tasks, RPC and Python automation hooks — point toward a version of Silhouette that fits more naturally into larger studio environments without requiring workarounds.

Website: borisfx.com/products/silhouette
Price: $103 (monthly subscription); $44.42 per month (annual subscription); $1,195 (permanent license)

Blackmagic Design’s DaVinci Resolve 21

There is a version of DaVinci Resolve’s history where it stays a color suite, and it’s extremely good at one thing and respected by colorists, used exclusively in finishing bays. That version of the story ended years ago, and DaVinci Resolve 21 is further proof that Blackmagic Design continues to evolve with the growing needs of the industry.

The new Photo page is the most attention-grabbing addition, and it earns the attention. Bringing Resolve’s node-based color pipeline to still images — with RAW support, LUT application, Resolve FX and full grading controls — makes sense in a way that feels inevitable once you see it. Photographers who may have been applying cinematic grades to stills through workarounds now have a tool designed for it. For artists who move fluidly between motion and stills, it removes the context-switching that used to require a separate application.

The AI tool set in Resolve 21 is worth close examination, because Blackmagic has been more careful than most about how it frames these features. IntelliSearch, AI Cinefocus, Face Age Transformer, Face Reshaper, UltraSharpen, Motion Deblur — these are not pitched as replacements for skilled work. They are aimed at the specific hours of production where the skilled work is being blocked by repetitive tasks. A tool that automates tedious cleanup is a different proposition than one that claims to make expertise optional.

Fusion gets a substantial expansion through the addition of the Krokodove tool set — more than 70 new graphic tools that expand motion graphics and make it easier to build reusable design elements. Combined with improvements to macros, text workflows, USD support and animation controls, Fusion is increasingly capable of holding its own alongside dedicated compositing and motion design environments. The question of whether artists should be doing effects work inside their NLE is becoming less interesting than the question of whether they even need to go elsewhere.

The Edit and Cut pages receive the kind of improvements that rarely make the press release but define whether a tool is actually enjoyable to use under pressure. Better keyframing, cleaner curve editing, more flexible timeline controls. These are accumulated refinements — the type that tend to reveal themselves only when you realize you have stopped fighting the software.

Colorists get improvements to the node graph organization, MultiMaster trim workflows, and color management updates that reinforce Resolve’s already strong position in finishing. That these updates feel incremental is not a criticism — when the foundation is this solid, incremental is the right pace.

Resolve 21 does not announce itself. It expands steadily, department by department, user case by user case — in the manner of software that has decided what it is trying to become and is not in a hurry about it.

Website: blackmagicdesign.com/products/davinciresolve
Price: Free (basic); $295 (Studio 21 version)

Todd Sheridan Perry is an award-winning VFX supervisor and digital artist whose recent credits include I’m a Virgo, For All Mankind and Black Panther. He can be reached at todd@teaspoonvfx.com.

items.headline: Venice-Set Reply AI Film Festival Unveils Finalists & Jury Featuring Gabriele Salvatores, Catherine Hardwicke & Jed Weintrob
items.body_text:
The Ukraine War, life without sight and an imaginary world where births have ceased are among the subjects of the ten films competing in the third edition of the Reply AI Film Festival which returns to the Venice Film Festival in September for its award ceremony.

The finalists, which were unveiled on Tuesday, have been selected from 3,000 short films experimenting made with AI technologies and tools and submitted in response to the competition’s 2026 theme of “Imaginatio Nova”. (scroll down for full list).

Oscar-winning director Gabriele Salvatores (Mediterraneo) presides over the jury also featuring filmmakers Rob Minkoff (The Lion King) and Catherine Hardwicke (Twilight) as well as Jed Weintrob, director and partner at creative studio 30 Ninjas alongside Doug Liman and Julina Tatlock; VFX Supervisor Giacomo Mineo (Oppenheimer, The Odyssey); former DreamWorks Animation and Netflix technology focused producer Christina Lee Storm and producer Nils Hartmann (Gomorrah, The Young Pope).
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Related Stories 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Festivals
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Rising Star Isiah Hilt On Catherine Hardwicke's 'Street Smart': "It's Like A Homeless 'Breakfast Club' Kind Of Vibe" - Bentonville Film Festival 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Podcast
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Graham Sibley Launches 'The Actor's Director Podcast'; John Ortiz, Catherine Hardwicke & Hikari Among Season 1 Guests

Further members include journalists Brian Welk and Denise Negri, Reply Chief Technology Officer Filippo Rizzante and Guillem Martinez Roura, AI & Robotics Lead on the “AI for Good” initiative of the United Nations’ International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and Jacopo Reale, who won the 2025 Reply prize for Love at First Sight.
 
 Watch on Deadline

Alongside the award for Best Short Film, the jury will present two special awards: the AI for Good Award for the short film that most effectively interprets the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and the Reply AI Studios Grand Prix for the project demonstrating the highest levels of innovation and excellence in the use of artificial intelligence throughout the creative process.

The winners will be announced on September 6 on the fringes of the Venice Film Festival, which this year is showcasing its first ever AI-made feature in Official Selection, Francesco Carrozzini’s documentary Be Brave about the founder of the Diesel fashion label Renzo Rosso.

The 2026 Reply AI Finalists

A Face Only A Mother Could Love
Creator: Robert Gaudette, AI filmmaker and director (Canada)
AI tools & technology: Grok, Nano Banana and Seedance
A solitary Parisian dancer convinced of his own beauty is approached by a woman who has secretly watched him for years

Centenarian Kindergarten
Creators: 2xLabs, a creative studio and collective of visual artists (China)
AI tools & technology: Nano Banana Pro and Jimeng SeedAce 2
In a dystopian future set in 2090, where births have ceased, four centenarians escape from a sterile facility in which AI assistants enforce compulsory happiness, in an attempt to reclaim their human imperfections.

GO HOME
Creator: Simone Paradiso, AI filmmaker and director (Italy)
AI tools and technology: Higgsfield Soul Cinema, GPT Image 2.0 and Seedance 2.0,
In New York in 1999, four teenagers discover a hidden military bunker, setting off on a science-fiction adventure involving mystery, fear and an enigmatic connection with a solitary girl in the group.

Kev
Creator: Mike Bennion, director (UK)
AI tools and technology: Midjourney, Nano Banana, Kling, Veo 3 and ElevenLabs
An intimate exploration of Kev’s personal experience of blindness, highlighting the people, relationships and aspects of everyday life that matter most to him.

Le Drip
Creators: Alex Naghavi and Ezra Li, visual artists and directors (Australia and U.S.)
AI tools and technology: Nano Banana, Claude, Seedance and Runway
The last day on Earth depicted through living oil paintings animated by dense, textured brushstrokes in motion, exploring human emotion.

Little Mes
Creators: Salad Collective, a creative studio and collective of directors (Spain)
AI tools and technology: Kling, Veo 3.1, Seedance and Suno
An inner monologue contemplating the many parallel and possible lives of a character, all coexisting at the same moment, exploring the tension between the life actually lived and the paths left open.

Once Upon a Time on the Dnieper River
Creator: Yi Wang, director (China)
AI tools and technology: Nano Banana, Dreamina, Vidu
Against the backdrop of the Russian-Ukrainian front, a soldier stranded on the banks of the Dnieper River is entrusted with a particularly sensitive and dangerous mission. Using

Passenger
Creator: Yuanbo Song, AI filmmaker and director (China)
AI tools and technology:
Mira, a tsunami survivor, restores her parents’ sculptures, but a mysterious intruder destroys them shortly before a devastating earthquake. Only later does she discover that he was actually trying to save her.

The Child of the Sea
Creator: Ibai Abad, stop-motion artist and director (Spain)
AI tools and technology: Magnific
A fish-boy embarks on a journey across 17th-century Spain to reunite with his mother, facing ridicule and fear in a tale exploring themes of diversity, belonging and acceptance.

Website
Creator: Jiaze Li, interactive media artist and director (China)
AI tools and technology: Veo 3, Runway, Kling and Seedance 2
A speculative science-fiction film exploring a platform capable of broadcasting impossible events from other worlds, where the very act of observation actively alters reality and influences culture.
